input.paper_title: Graph-Aware Prompting for Reliable Section Generation
input.paper_venue: ACL Workshop on Natural Language Generation
input.paper_abstract: We present a graph-guided prompting workflow for long-form scientific writing that prioritizes evidence and citation consistency. Our method constructs a document graph that encodes section dependencies and uses strict JSON schemas and evidence-aware prompts to generate and validate individual sections. At generation time, the system (1) builds a section graph and schedules leaf-first writing, (2) retrieves and injects relevant evidence for each section, (3) produces JSON-constrained section outputs, and (4) assembles a LaTeX manuscript with refs.bib. We evaluate the approach by comparing it to a baseline linear prompting pipeline on two topical domains, measuring citation coverage, hallucination rate, and reviewer-style scores. Results show improved citation coverage and reduced unsupported assertions while keeping edits and post-hoc audits straightforward via machine-readable outputs. We intentionally state conservative claims and require explicit source citations for all factual assertions. The paper contributes practical artifacts: a graph-based section scheduler, an evidence-injection protocol per section, and an audit-friendly JSON output format that integrates with standard LaTeX/bib workflows. Our experiments use internal notes and a small curated PDF set where available; metrics focus on citation fidelity and factual consistency rather than broad generalization.

input.section_summary: Specify the strict JSON schema for each generated section (fields, types, required citation/evidence fields, machine-checkable constraints), validation procedure, and how JSON outputs facilitate edits and audits.

output:
Note on grounding. The text below describes the intended JSON schema and associated validation logic at a conceptual level. Because no retrieved excerpts or run artifacts were provided for this section, the descriptions are presented as general background knowledge and design proposals; they should be instantiated or revised once concrete schema examples, prior outputs, or validator logs are available.

Purpose and design goals (general background knowledge)
- The JSON schema for each generated section is intended to (1) make section contents machine-checkable, (2) require explicit links from factual assertions to evidence, and (3) produce outputs that can be deterministically assembled into LaTeX + refs.bib and audited or edited programmatically.
- The schema is designed to support conservative generation workflows: mandatory evidence fields for factual claims, explicit metadata for provenance, and structured validation results that record any unsupported assertions.

Proposed top-level structure (general background knowledge)
- section_id (string, required): stable identifier for the section node (e.g., ``3.2'' or ``methods-evidence'').
- title (string, required): human-readable section title.
- body (string, required): the section text, preferably in Markdown or LaTeX fragments depending on downstream assembly rules.
- claims (array of claim objects, required): fine-grained, machine-addressable assertions extracted or generated for this section (see claim object below).
- references (array of reference objects, required if any claims cite external material): bibliographic records intended for refs.bib assembly.
- dependencies (array of section_id strings, optional): explicit upstream section nodes that this section depends on for background facts or definitions.
- provenance (object, required): metadata about how this JSON was produced (model identifier, prompt template identifier, generation timestamp).
- validation (object, required): results of automated checks (schema validation status, evidence-coverage summary, unsupported-claim detections, and any validation error messages).
- editor_notes (string, optional): free-text field for human editors indicating required interventions.

Claim object (general background knowledge)
- id (string, required): unique claim identifier within the section.
- text (string, required): the claim phrased as a single declarative sentence or short paragraph.
- claim_type (enum: [``definition'',``measurement'',``method'',``finding'',``background''], optional): coarse label to guide evidence requirements.
- factuality_flag (enum: [``factual'',``speculative'',``opinion''], required): indicates whether the claim must be backed by external evidence; conservative workflows should treat ``factual'' as requiring non-empty evidence_ids.
- evidence_ids (array of evidence identifiers, required if factuality_flag == ``factual''): references to evidence items (these identifiers must map to entries in the references field or to retrieval-result identifiers).
- citation_anchors (array of small strings, optional): textual anchors used in-line to mark where citations should appear in assembled text.
- confidence_score (number, optional): model-reported confidence in the claim; recorded but not used as sole validation logic.
- validation (object, required): per-claim validation outcomes (e.g., evidence_present: bool, unsupported_reason: string|null).

Reference object (general background knowledge)
- ref_id (string, required): stable id used by evidence_ids and for refs.bib assembly.
- bibtex (string, optional but preferred): raw BibTeX entry for assembly.
- title, authors, year, url (fields optional): parsed bibliographic metadata for human review.
- source_id (string, optional): identifier linking back to the retrieval system (e.g., index id or provenance token).

Validation procedure (general background knowledge)
- Syntactic validation: enforce JSON Schema conformance (required fields present and types correct). Failures are reported in validation.schema_errors.
- Evidence-coverage checks: for each claim with factuality_flag == ``factual'', require evidence_ids to be non-empty and map to valid reference objects. Missing evidence yields validation.evidence_coverage_failures.
- Unsupported-claim detection: run an automated heuristic or classifier (record outcome in claim.validation.unsupported_reason) to flag claims that lack adequate support in the injected evidence. The schema records these flags for downstream human review.
- Citation formatting checks: ensure all ref_id values referenced in claims appear in references and that a bibtex or equivalent entry is available for each. Missing bibtex entries are recorded as validation.bib_missing.
- Assembly pre-flight: confirm that required fields for LaTeX assembly (body, references with bibtex, and citation anchors) are present; otherwise, mark as assembly_blockers with explicit messages.

How the schema facilitates edits and audits (general background knowledge)
- Machine-readable claims enable targeted human review: auditors can review only claim objects flagged as unsupported rather than scanning full text.
- Deterministic refs.bib assembly: references are stored as structured records so refs.bib can be emitted programmatically, reducing manual copy errors and improving reproducibility.
- Diff-friendly outputs: JSON outputs can be diffed across generation iterations to isolate changes introduced by model re-runs or prompt edits.
- Traceability: provenance fields link each section to the prompt templates and retrieval artifacts used, supporting reproducible debugging and intervention.

Minimal implementation notes (general background knowledge)
- Use an explicit JSON Schema document to enforce type constraints and required fields at generation time; reject or flag outputs that do not validate.
- Treat claim-level evidence linkage as the primary signal for downstream acceptance: sections with any factual claims lacking evidence should be routed for human intervention before assembly.
- Record all validation failures and keep a validation.log that is shipped with the generated manuscript artifacts for auditing.

Limitations and need for grounded examples
- The above structure is a design proposal and does not include concrete schema files, example generated outputs, or empirical thresholds for automated unsupported-claim detectors. These artifacts are required to finalize the schema and to implement effective validators.
- To proceed from this conceptual schema to an operational one, we request the following retrievals or artifacts (please supply as excerpts or run artifacts):
  - Example JSON outputs from prior generation runs (both passing and failing validation).
  - Any existing JSON Schema files or validator implementations used in related pipeline steps.
  - Logs or annotations from human adjudicators marking unsupported claims (to inform the unsupported-claim detector).
  - Sample refs.bib outputs produced by the assembly step and mapping between ref_id and retrieval-source identifiers.
  - Prompt templates that instruct the generation model to emit the JSON structure (to ensure the schema fields align with model output capabilities).

Concluding remark
- Once concrete examples and validator artifacts are available, the proposed fields and validation logic above can be formalized into a machine-enforceable JSON Schema and integrated into the graph-aware prompting pipeline.
